original_value: People increasingly use social media to report emergencies, seek help or share information during disasters, which makes social networks an important tool for disaster management. To meet these time-critical needs, we present a weakly supervised approach for rapidly building high-quality classifiers that label each individual Twitter message with fine-grained event categories. Most importantly, we propose a novel method to create high-quality labeled data in a timely manner that automatically clusters tweets containing an event keyword and asks a domain expert to disambiguate event word senses and label clusters quickly. In addition, to process extremely noisy and often rather short user-generated messages, we enrich tweet representations using preceding context tweets and reply tweets in building event recognition classifiers. The evaluation on two hurricanes, Harvey and Florence, shows that using only 1-2 person-hours of human supervision, the rapidly trained weakly supervised classifiers outperform supervised classifiers trained using more than ten thousand annotated tweets created in over 50 person-hours.

result.paraphrase: People increasingly turn to social media to report emergencies, ask for help, or share information during disasters, making social networks an important disaster-management tool. To address these time-sensitive needs, we introduce a weakly supervised method for quickly building high-quality classifiers that assign fine-grained event categories to individual Twitter messages. Most importantly, we present a new approach for timely creation of high-quality labeled data that automatically groups tweets containing an event keyword and has a domain expert quickly disambiguate event word senses and label the clusters. We also improve event-recognition classifiers for extremely noisy and often very short user-generated messages by enriching tweet representations with preceding context tweets and reply tweets. Evaluation on Hurricanes Harvey and Florence shows that, with only 1–2 person-hours of human supervision, the rapidly trained weakly supervised classifiers outperform supervised classifiers trained on more than ten thousand annotated tweets produced in over 50 person-hours.
